The papersThe code

Ensemble networks for tumour classes, dug back up.

We rebuilt the lost Matlab method from the paper and reran it on the seven Kent Ridge datasets. Of 19 results we tried, 8 came back exactly, 2 agree, 6 partly agree and 3 differ.

Table 2, our methods: test-set accuracy (ALL-AML, lung, prostate)Partly agrees1 of 3 values
  • ALL-AML test accuracy, % (33 of 34 correct): paper 100, ours 97.06
  • Lung test accuracy, % (149 of 149 correct): paper 100, ours 100
  • Prostate test accuracy, % (31 of 34 correct): paper 97.06, ours 91.18
Lung comes back (149 of 149). Prostate: 31 of 34 against 33; scaling each array to the same mean intensity, a step the paper does not mention, gives exactly 33 of 34 on all five seeds, so the gap is likely how the test experiment, about 12 times brighter than the training arrays, was handled. ALL-AML: 33 of 34 against 34; the same test sample (31st in the file) is wrong in every seed and every hypothesis test (only the AdaBoost control gets it right, missing another).

Lung comes back (32 of 32). ALL-AML 37 of 38 against 38 (training sample 29 is wrong in both runs we made), prostate 95 of 102 against 98. Weight decay 0.1 gains one prostate sample (96); no other setting we tried moves either.

Python package cfsenn and its tutorialAgrees

The main claim holds in part: our ensemble beats the bagged trees on all three test sets and each Discussion control classifies worse, but it only ties the best cited method on ALL-AML, its prostate LOOCV is not below its test accuracy, and it falls short of Cho and Won's DLBCL split; the causes are one ALL-AML test sample that every seed and hypothesis test misses, the unscaled prostate test arrays and the unlisted 22/25 split.

What came back

Table 1
All seven datasets have the paper's genes and samples, class by class.
Lung and MLL
Every test sample right: 149 of 149 and 15 of 15, on every seed for MLL.
DLBCL
46 of 47 by LOOCV and 45 of 47 by 10-fold CV, as printed.
The method
cfsenn, a Python package with an executed tutorial.

What stayed buried

  • The authors' Matlab code and how they trained the networks.
  • How the genes were clustered for the third feature set.
  • The samples of Cho and Won's DLBCL split.
  • Why one ALL-AML test sample and three colon samples stay wrong for us.

The main claim holds in part: our ensemble beats the bagged trees on all three test sets and each Discussion control classifies worse, but it only ties the best cited method on ALL-AML, its prostate LOOCV is not below its test accuracy, and it falls short of Cho and Won's DLBCL split; the causes are one ALL-AML test sample that every seed and hypothesis test misses, the unscaled prostate test arrays and the unlisted 22/25 split.

What we matched

The datasets came back whole from a mirror of the lost Kent Ridge repository. Where our counts differ, they differ by one to three samples.
